questions.q: What is the peak age of incidence for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) in pediatric patients?
questions.hint: Early childhood peak between 2 and 5 years of age.
questions.explanation: Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) displays a prominent early childhood peak, presenting most frequently between 2 and 5 years of age.

questions.q: What proportion of all pediatric leukemia cases is represented by Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)?
questions.hint: ALL accounts for 75% to 80% of childhood leukemias.
questions.explanation: ALL is the single most common childhood malignancy, accounting for 75% to 80% of all pediatric leukemia cases.

questions.q: According to WHO diagnostic criteria, what minimum percentage of blast cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood is required to diagnose Acute Leukemia?
questions.hint: WHO criteria require ≥20% blasts.
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines acute leukemia by the demonstration of 20% or more immature lymphoblasts or myeloblasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

questions.q: Which cell lineage accounts for approximately 85% of childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia cases?
questions.hint: Precursor B-cell ALL (B-ALL) makes up ~85% of ALL.
questions.explanation: Precursor B-cell ALL (B-ALL) comprises approximately 85% of pediatric ALL cases, whereas T-cell ALL (T-ALL) accounts for the remaining 15%.

questions.q: What classic clinical triad results directly from bone marrow failure due to leukemic blast overcrowding?
questions.hint: Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia from marrow replacement.
questions.explanation: Replacement of normal marrow elements by proliferating leukemic blasts impairs hematopoiesis, presenting as anemia, thrombocytopenic bleeding, and neutropenic fever.

questions.q: Which diagnostic surface antigen marker is expressed on B-lymphoblasts and historically designated as CALLA (Common ALL Antigen)?
questions.hint: CD10 is CALLA.
questions.explanation: CD10 is known as the Common Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Antigen (CALLA) and is expressed on the majority of precursor B-ALL lymphoblasts.

questions.q: What percentage of pediatric leukemia cases is represented by Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)?
questions.hint: AML accounts for ~15% to 20% of pediatric leukemias.
questions.explanation: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) constitutes approximately 15% to 20% of childhood leukemias but carries a higher proportion of leukemia-related mortality.

questions.q: Which enzyme marker, detected by immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry, confirms myeloid lineage in Acute Myeloid Leukemia?
questions.hint: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) confirms myeloid lineage.
questions.explanation: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is an enzyme specific to the myeloid lineage; its positivity distinguishes AML from ALL.

questions.q: Which sub-type of ALL typically presents in older adolescent males with a rapidly enlarging anterior mediastinal mass and high leukocyte counts?
questions.hint: T-ALL often presents in adolescent boys with a mediastinal mass and high WBC.
questions.explanation: T-ALL predominantly affects older adolescent boys, classically presenting with hyperleukocytosis and an anterior mediastinal mass causing airway or superior vena cava compression.

questions.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic procedure required to confirm pediatric leukemia and perform lineage immunophenotyping?
options: A) Peripheral blood film examination only
B) Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
questions.hint: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
questions.explanation: Although peripheral blood may show circulating blasts, definitive diagnosis, cytogenetic risk stratification, and flow cytometry require a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.

questions.q: Which chromosomal cytogenetic abnormality represents the single most common favorable genetic alteration in pediatric B-ALL, present in 25–30% of cases?
options: C) High Hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes, often with trisomies 4, 10, and 17)
questions.hint: High hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes) is a common favorable B-ALL finding.
questions.explanation: High hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes per leukemic cell) carries an excellent treatment response and favorable prognosis, accounting for nearly one-third of B-ALL cases.

questions.q: Which translocation fusion gene, present in 20–25% of pediatric B-ALL cases, confers a highly favorable prognosis and high cure rates with standard chemotherapy?
questions.hint: ETV6::RUNX1 [t(12;21)] is favorable in B-ALL.
questions.explanation: The ETV6::RUNX1 cryptic translocation [t(12;21)(p13;q22)] is the most frequent structural rearrangement in childhood B-ALL and is associated with superior event-free survival.

questions.q: Which cytogenetic abnormality defines the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph+) in ALL and mandates the addition of a Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (TKI) to chemotherapy?
options: A) Translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) creating the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene
questions.hint: t(9;22) / BCR::ABL1 = Philadelphia chromosome; treat with a TKI.
questions.explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) generates the constitutively active BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase driver, requiring targeted TKI therapy (Imatinib or Dasatinib).

questions.q: What specific chromosomal rearrangement is uniquely characteristic of infant leukemia (<1 year of age) and carries a high risk of induction failure and early relapse?
options: B) KMT2A (MLL) gene rearrangements at chromosome 11q23
questions.hint: KMT2A (MLL) rearrangements at 11q23 in infants <1 year.
questions.explanation: Rearrangements of the KMT2A (MLL) gene at 11q23 occur in >70–80% of infant ALL cases, representing an aggressive, chemoresistant leukemia subtype.

questions.q: Which acute leukemia subtype presents with severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) due to the release of pro-coagulant tissue factors from leukemic promyelocytes?
options: C) Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3) with t(15;17) PML::RARA
questions.hint: APL (AML M3) with t(15;17) PML::RARA causes severe DIC.
questions.explanation: APL (AML M3) is characterized by abnormal promyelocytes packed with Auer rods that trigger life-threatening DIC, requiring immediate start of All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA).

questions.q: What underlying constitutional genetic disorder carries a 10- to 20-fold increased risk of developing childhood acute leukemia, including a unique predisposition to Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AML M7)?
questions.hint: Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
questions.explanation: Children with Down syndrome have a markedly increased risk of ALL and a specific predisposition to Transient Myeloproliferative Disorder (TMD) and Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AML M7) in early infancy.

questions.q: Which immunophenotypic marker profile specifically establishes the diagnosis of precursor T-cell ALL (T-ALL)?
options: A) Cytoplasmic or surface CD3, CD7, CD2, and CD5
B) CD19, CD10, CD22, and CD79a
C) CD13, CD33, CD117, and MPO
questions.hint: CD3 (cytoplasmic or surface) plus CD7, CD2, and CD5.
questions.explanation: T-ALL lymphoblasts express pan-T-cell markers, with cytoplasmic or surface CD3 being the definitive lineage-specific marker, alongside CD7, CD2, and CD5.

questions.q: What is a Myeloid Sarcoma (Chloroma)?
options: A) A benign vascular tumor of the liver
B) An extramedullary tumor mass composed of leukemic myeloid blasts occurring in soft tissues, bone, or orbits
C) A fungal infection occurring during neutropenia
D) A primary brain tumor originating in astrocytes
questions.hint: Extramedullary mass of myeloid blasts (chloroma).
questions.explanation: A myeloid sarcoma (chloroma) is a localized extramedullary tumor mass of immature myeloid blasts that may precede or accompany marrow involvement in AML.

questions.q: What structural cytogenetic rearrangements in AML belong to the 'Core-Binding Factor' (CBF) category and confer a favorable outcome?
options: C) Translocation t(8;21)(q22;q22) [RUNX1::RUNX1T1] and Inversion inv(16)(p13q22) [CBFB::MYH11]
D) FLT3-ITD mutation with high allelic ratio
questions.hint: t(8;21) and inv(16) are core-binding factor AMLs with favorable prognosis.
questions.explanation: Core-binding factor (CBF) AMLs, involving t(8;21) or inv(16), disrupt transcription factor complexes and carry a favorable prognosis in pediatric AML.

questions.q: How is Central Nervous System (CNS) status classified as 'CNS-3' (CNS leukemia) upon diagnostic lumbar puncture?
options: A) Absence of blasts in CSF with WBC < 5/µL
B) Presence of cytospin-positive blasts with WBC < 5/µL (CNS-2)
C) Traumatic lumbar puncture with blood contamination
D) Demonstration of cytospin-positive leukemic blasts in CSF with a CSF WBC count ≥ 5/µL, or clinical cranial nerve palsy
questions.hint: CSF WBC ≥ 5/µL with blasts present, or cranial nerve palsy.
questions.explanation: CNS-3 (active CNS leukemia) is defined by ≥ 5 WBCs/µL in CSF with positive blast cytology, or the presence of a leukemic cranial nerve palsy.

questions.q: What characteristic skeletal symptom in young children with ALL often leads to initial misdiagnosis as juvenile idiopathic arthritis or osteomyelitis?
options: A) Severe bone pain, nocturnal leg pain, limping, or refusal to bear weight due to leukemic marrow expansion
B) Painless hyperostosis of the calvarium
C) Symmetrical bowing of the tibiae
questions.hint: Bone pain, night pain, or limping from marrow expansion.
questions.explanation: Leukemic expansion within the medullary cavity and periosteal infiltration cause intense bone and joint pain, frequently presenting as limping or refusal to walk.

questions.q: What physical examination finding defines extramedullary leukemic relapse or sanctuary site involvement in male patients with B-ALL?
options: B) Painless, hard, asymmetrical enlargement of one or both testes
questions.hint: Painless, firm enlargement of a testis.
questions.explanation: The testes serve as an anatomical sanctuary site for leukemic cells due to the blood-testis barrier; involvement presents as painless, firm testicular enlargement.

questions.q: What is Minimal Residual Disease (MRD), and why is it measured during acute leukemia therapy?
options: A) The persistent presence of physical symptoms after 1 year
B) The size of the spleen measured on ultrasound
C) Sub-microscopic leukemic cell persistence (below morphological detection) measured by flow cytometry or molecular methods, serving as the single strongest predictor of relapse risk
D) The count of mature neutrophils remaining in blood
questions.hint: Sub-microscopic residual blasts; strongest predictor of relapse risk.
questions.explanation: MRD quantifies residual leukemic blasts down to 10⁻⁴ (0.01%) or lower at key treatment milestones (e.g., end of induction), guiding risk-directed treatment escalation.

questions.q: What threshold of End-of-Induction Minimal Residual Disease (MRD) by flow cytometry is universally used to define MRD-positivity requiring treatment intensification?
options: D) ≥0.01% (1 leukemic cell per 10,000 normal cells)
questions.explanation: An end-of-induction MRD level ≥ 0.01% (0.0001) identifies patients with high risk of relapse who require treatment intensification or stem cell transplantation.

questions.q: Which oncological emergency manifests in pediatric ALL with hyperleukocytosis (WBC > 100,000/µL) causing microvascular sludging, neurological deficits, and respiratory distress?
questions.hint: Hyperleukocytosis (>100,000/µL) causing microvascular sludging = leukostasis.
questions.explanation: Extremely high circulating blast counts (>100,000/µL) increase blood viscosity, leading to microvascular leukostasis, hypoxia, CNS hemorrhage, and respiratory failure.

questions.q: What metabolic derangements constitute the classic biochemical diagnostic tetrad of Acute Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)?
options: A) Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypercalcemia
B) Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Hyperuricemia, and Hypocalcemia
C) Hypernatremia, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia, and hypokalemia
D) Hypoglycemia, hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia, and hyponatremia
questions.hint: High K+, high PO4, high uric acid, and low Ca2+.
questions.explanation: TLS results from rapid release of intracellular contents from lysed malignant cells, causing high potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, which secondarily precipitates serum calcium (hypocalcemia).

questions.q: Which pharmacological agent is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that rapidly breaks down uric acid into soluble allantoin to prevent acute renal failure in severe Tumor Lysis Syndrome?
questions.hint: Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase.
questions.explanation: Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) directly degrades existing uric acid into highly soluble allantoin, providing rapid clearance in patients with high TLS risk or established hyperuricemia.

questions.q: What initial diagnostic imaging study is mandatory in any child presenting with suspected T-ALL or severe leukocytosis before performing sedation or procedures?
options: D) Upright Chest X-ray (to rule out a mediastinal mass and airway compression)
questions.hint: Upright chest X-ray to check for an anterior mediastinal mass.
questions.explanation: An upright chest X-ray must be obtained immediately to detect anterior mediastinal mass expansion, which risks fatal airway collapse or cardiac arrest under sedation.

questions.q: What cutaneous physical manifestation of leukemia occurs predominantly in congenital or infant leukemia, presenting as firm, violaceous dermal papules and nodules?
questions.hint: 'Blueberry muffin' lesions (leukemia cutis).
questions.explanation: Infiltration of leukemic blasts into the skin of neonates and infants produces characteristic dark blue/purple dermal nodules, known as 'blueberry muffin' lesions.

questions.q: What specific clinical risk factors categorize a child with B-ALL as 'High Risk' under National Cancer Institute (NCI) criteria at diagnosis?
options: A) Age < 1 year or > 10 years, OR initial White Blood Cell (WBC) count ≥ 50,000/µL
B) Age 2 to 5 years with initial WBC < 10,000/µL
C) Female sex with isolated anemia
D) Normal cytogenetics with negative MRD
questions.hint: Age <1 or ≥10 years, or WBC ≥ 50,000/µL.
questions.explanation: NCI risk stratification for B-ALL defines High Risk as age <1 year or ≥10 years, or an initial WBC count ≥ 50,000/µL at presentation.

questions.q: What are the standard chemotherapy drugs that comprise the 3- or 4-drug Induction regimen for pediatric B-ALL?
options: C) Vincristine, a Corticosteroid (Dexamethasone or Prednisone), L-Asparaginase (Pegaspargase), +/- an Anthracycline (Daunorubicin)
questions.hint: Vincristine, corticosteroid, L-asparaginase/pegaspargase, +/- daunorubicin.
questions.explanation: Standard ALL Induction utilizes Vincristine, Dexamethasone/Prednisone, and Pegaspargase (with Daunorubicin added for NCI High-Risk cases) to achieve complete morphologic remission.

questions.q: What is the primary goal of the INDUCTION phase of chemotherapy in pediatric ALL treatment?
options: A) Eradication of late relapsed clones after 3 years
C) Elimination of mature red blood cells
D) Achievement of Complete Morphologic Remission (defined as <5% leukemic blasts in bone marrow with restoration of normal hematopoiesis)
questions.hint: Complete morphologic remission (<5% marrow blasts and recovery of normal hematopoiesis).
questions.explanation: The Induction phase aims to clear >99% of initial systemic leukemic burden and restore normal hematopoiesis, defined by <5% marrow blasts.

questions.q: Which targeted monoclonal antibody is a Bispecific T-cell Engager (BiTE) that binds CD19 on B-ALL lymphoblasts and CD3 on T-cells, approved for relapsed or MRD-positive B-ALL?
questions.hint: Blinatumomab engages CD3 T-cells against CD19 B-ALL blasts.
questions.explanation: Blinatumomab engages autologous cytotoxic T-cells (via CD3) to lyse CD19-positive B-ALL blasts, proving highly effective in clearing resistant MRD and relapsed B-ALL.

questions.q: What central maintenance chemotherapy regimen is administered orally over a duration of 2 to 3 years to maintain long-term remission in pediatric ALL?
options: A) Daily IV Cytarabine and weekly IV Cisplatin
B) Daily oral 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) and weekly oral Methotrexate, supplemented with periodic pulses of Vincristine and Corticosteroids
questions.hint: Daily oral 6-MP and weekly oral methotrexate (plus vincristine/steroid pulses).
questions.explanation: ALL Maintenance therapy relies on backbone anti-metabolite therapy with daily oral 6-MP and weekly oral Methotrexate over a total treatment duration of 2 to 3 years.

questions.q: What pharmacogenomic enzyme deficiency impairs the metabolism of 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP), predisposing patients to life-threatening myelosuppression unless the dose is drastically reduced?
options: C) Thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) or NUDT15 deficiency
questions.hint: TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency.
questions.explanation: TPMT and NUDT15 enzymes metabolize thiopurines (6-MP); inherited deficiencies cause accumulation of toxic thioguanine nucleotides, requiring dose reductions.

questions.q: Which therapy is indicated for treatment of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, t(15;17)) to induce terminal differentiation of promyelocytic blasts without causing cell lysis?
options: D) All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA) combined with Arsenic Trioxide (ATO)
questions.hint: ATRA plus arsenic trioxide (ATO).
questions.explanation: ATRA and ATO target the PML::RARA fusion protein, driving malignant promyelocytes to differentiate into mature granulocytes and achieving cure rates >90%.

questions.q: What targeted Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell cellular therapy is FDA-approved for pediatric patients with relapsed or refractory B-ALL up to age 25?
questions.hint: Tisagenlecleucel (anti-CD19 CAR-T).
questions.explanation: Tisagenlecleucel uses autologous T-cells genetically engineered with an anti-CD19 CAR to target refractory/relapsed B-ALL, inducing durable remissions.

questions.q: Why is Intrathecal Chemotherapy (e.g., Intrathecal Methotrexate, Cytarabine, and Hydrocortisone) administered to ALL patients across all phases of treatment?
options: A) To prevent local systemic skin toxicity
B) To provide CNS prophylaxis and eradicate sanctuary leukemic cells behind the blood-brain barrier
C) To stimulate endogenous bone marrow recovery
D) To prevent renal calculus formation
questions.hint: CNS prophylaxis across the blood-brain barrier.
questions.explanation: Systemic chemotherapy poorly penetrates the blood-brain barrier; routine intrathecal injections prevent central nervous system relapse.

questions.q: What toxic side effect is uniquely associated with L-Asparaginase (or Pegaspargase) therapy in pediatric ALL protocols?
options: C) Pancreatitis, thrombosis/coagulopathy (due to antithrombin III depletion), and hypersensitivity reactions
D) Cardiomyopathy with left ventricular failure
questions.hint: Pancreatitis, thrombosis/coagulopathy, and hypersensitivity.
questions.explanation: Asparaginase depletes systemic asparagine and hepatic protein synthesis, predisposing patients to acute pancreatitis, hypofibrinogenemia, thrombosis, and allergic reactions.

questions.q: What empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy must be initiated within 1 hour in a pediatric leukemia patient presenting with Febrile Neutropenia (Fever ≥ 38.3°C and Absolute Neutrophil Count < 500/µL)?
options: D) Monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Cefepime, Piperacillin-Tazobactam, or Meropenem)
questions.hint: Prompt antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem).
questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia is a life-threatening emergency; immediate empiric broad-spectrum coverage against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Gram-negative bacilli is required.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with 3 weeks of fatigue, pallor, petechiae, nocturnal leg pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, Hb 6.5 g/dL, platelets 14,000/µL, WBC 42,000/µL, and 55% circulating lymphoblasts. Identify the diagnosis, bone marrow blast cutoff, and the four sequential chemotherapy phases.
options: A) Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL); ≥20% bone marrow blasts; Induction, Consolidation/Intensification, Interim Maintenance, and Maintenance
B) Aplastic Anemia; 0% blasts; Antithymocyte globulin, Cyclosporine, Steroids, and Transfusion
C) Infectious Mononucleosis; <5% blasts; Rest, Hydration, Analgesics, and Steroids
D) Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP); Normal marrow; IVIG alone
questions.hint: Cytopenias + bone pain + lymphoblasts = ALL (≥20% blasts); 4 phases: induction, consolidation, interim maintenance, maintenance.
questions.explanation: Bone marrow failure + bone pain + circulating blasts indicates ALL. Confirmation requires ≥20% blasts on bone marrow evaluation. Standard management proceeds through Induction, Consolidation, Interim Maintenance, and Maintenance.

questions.q: A 13-year-old boy presents with severe dyspnea, orthopnea, facial swelling, distended neck veins, stridor, a massive anterior mediastinal mass on CXR, and WBC 148,000/µL with 80% CD3+/CD7+ blasts. Diagnose the subtype, acute emergency, and critical sedation/procedure precaution.
options: A) Precursor B-ALL; Tumor Lysis Syndrome; Perform immediate spinal anesthesia
B) T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (T-ALL); Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome and Airway Compression; Avoid deep sedation or general anesthesia due to risk of fatal airway collapse
C) Acute Myeloid Leukemia; Leukostasis; Perform immediate sternotomy
D) Hodgkin Lymphoma; Cardiac tamponade; Administer high-dose IV fluid boluses
questions.hint: CD3+/CD7+ + mediastinal mass + SVC/airway signs = T-ALL; avoid sedation/anesthesia due to airway collapse risk.
questions.explanation: T-ALL in adolescent boys classically presents with mediastinal mass causing SVC syndrome and tracheal compression. Muscle relaxation during sedation causes loss of chest wall tone and fatal airway obstruction; procedures must be delayed until steroid/chemo shrinkage.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy with B-ALL on Day 3 of Induction has oliguria, K+ 6.4 mmol/L, uric acid 12.8 mg/dL, phosphorus 8.5 mg/dL, and ionized calcium 0.85 mmol/L. Identify the emergency, pathophysiological trigger, and immediate management.
options: A) Acute Glomerulonephritis; Immune complex deposition; Give IV corticosteroids
B) Diabetic Ketoacidosis; Insulin deficiency; Start insulin infusion

C) Laboratory Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS); Massive rapid release of intracellular electrolytes and nucleic acids from lysed blasts; Administer aggressive IV hydration, Rasburicase (or Allopurinol), and manage hyperkalemia
D) Adrenal insufficiency; Adrenal hemorrhage; Give stress-dose hydrocortisone
questions.hint: High K+, high PO4, high uric acid, low Ca2+ = TLS; treat with hydration, rasburicase/allopurinol, and hyperkalemia care.
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia define Tumor Lysis Syndrome. Management mandates hyperhydration without potassium, Rasburicase to clear uric acid, and cardiac monitoring.

questions.q: A 2-year-old girl with NCI standard-risk B-ALL has 1.5% morphologic marrow blasts at end of Induction, but flow cytometry MRD is 0.4%. Interpret the MRD result, how it changes risk/therapy, and what targeted immunotherapy applies.
options: A) MRD is negative; Stop chemotherapy early
B) MRD is invalid; Repeat bone marrow in 1 year
C) Patient has relapsed; Switch to end-of-life palliative care
D) Patient is MRD-positive (≥0.01%), indicating high risk of relapse; Therapy must be intensified (re-stratified to High-Risk protocol) and Blinatumomab or CAR-T considered
questions.hint: MRD ≥0.01% predicts relapse; intensify therapy and consider blinatumomab or CAR-T.
questions.explanation: An end-of-induction MRD ≥ 0.01% (here 0.4%) is the strongest predictor of relapse. Morphologic remission alone is insufficient; the patient must be re-stratified to intensified chemotherapy and evaluated for Blinatumomab or CAR T-cell therapy.

questions.q: An 8-year-old child has severe bleeding, hypergranular promyelocytes with Auer rods ('faggot cells'), PT 24s, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL, high D-dimer, and t(15;17)(q22;q12). Diagnose the subtype, hematological emergency, and immediate targeted agent.
options: A) Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3); Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC); All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA)
B) Pre-B ALL; Immune Thrombocytopenia; High-dose IVIG
C) Chronic Myeloid Leukemia; Blast crisis; Imatinib mesylate
D) T-ALL; Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura; Plasma exchange
questions.hint: Auer rods/faggot cells + t(15;17) + coagulopathy = APL with DIC; start ATRA immediately.
questions.explanation: Promyelocytes with Auer rods and t(15;17) define APL (AML M3). Granule release causes severe DIC. Immediate administration of ATRA promotes promyelocyte differentiation and resolves coagulopathy.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy in remission on Maintenance B-ALL therapy for 18 months develops painless, firm 3 cm left testicular enlargement. What is the primary suspicion, why does the testis act this way, and what confirms diagnosis?
options: A) Hydrocele; Fluid accumulation; Transillumination test
B) Extramedullary Testicular Relapse of B-ALL; The blood-testis barrier acts as an anatomical sanctuary site shielding blasts from systemic chemotherapy; Bilateral testicular wedge biopsy
C) Epididymitis; Bacterial infection; Urine culture
D) Testicular torsion; Vascular occlusion; Emergency Doppler ultrasound
questions.hint: Painless firm testicular enlargement in ALL = testicular relapse (blood-testis sanctuary); confirm with biopsy.
questions.explanation: Painless firm testicular swelling during or after ALL therapy indicates isolated testicular relapse. The blood-testis barrier shields blasts from systemically administered drugs. Diagnosis is confirmed by testicular biopsy.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant has hepatosplenomegaly, 'blueberry muffin' skin lesions, WBC 180,000/µL with 75% lymphoblasts, and KMT2A (MLL) translocation t(4;11)(q21;q23). Classify the presentation, KMT2A prognosis in infants, and consolidation modality.
options: A) Standard-Risk Infant B-ALL; Favorable prognosis; Maintenance therapy alone
B) Transient Myeloproliferative Disorder; Self-limiting; Observation only
C) High-Risk Infant ALL with KMT2A rearrangement; Highly aggressive with poor prognosis and high relapse rates; Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT)
D) Congenital CMV infection; Excellent prognosis; Oral ganciclovir
questions.hint: Infant <1 year + KMT2A rearrangement = high-risk, poor prognosis; often needs allogeneic HSCT.
questions.explanation: Infant ALL (<1 year) with KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement represents an exceptionally high-risk entity characterized by hyperleukocytosis, extramedullary disease, and chemoresistance, often requiring allogeneic HSCT.

questions.q: Comparing pediatric B-ALL vs pediatric AML: which accounts for ~80% of cases with >90% cure rates using 2–3 years of maintenance-based therapy, and which accounts for 15–20% with MPO/Auer rods and ~65–70% survival?
options: D) 1. Precursor B-ALL; 2. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
questions.hint: 1. Precursor B-ALL; 2. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).
questions.explanation: B-ALL comprises 80% of pediatric leukemias with cure rates >90% using 2-3 years of maintenance-based chemotherapy. AML accounts for 15-20% of cases, features MPO/Auer rods, requires intense myeloablative cycles, and has survival rates around 65-70%.

questions.q: A 7-year-old on 6-MP and weekly methotrexate Maintenance develops severe prolonged pancytopenia (ANC < 100/µL, platelets 10,000/µL) and mucositis with a hypocellular marrow. What pharmacogenomic defect explains this, what test is done, and how is 6-MP adjusted?
options: A) Homozygous Thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) or NUDT15 deficiency; Genotypic/phenotypic TPMT testing; Reduce 6-MP dose by 90% (to 10% of standard dose)
B) G6PD deficiency; Fluorescent spot test; Stop Methotrexate
C) DPD deficiency; Plasma uracil test; Double the 6-MP dose
D) Factor V Leiden; Activated protein C ratio; Give IV heparin
questions.hint: Homozygous TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency -> test TPMT/NUDT15 and cut 6-MP dose by ~90%.
questions.explanation: Patients with homozygous TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency cannot metabolize 6-MP, leading to toxic accumulation of 6-thioguanine nucleotides and severe marrow aplasia. Dose must be reduced by ~90%.

questions.q: For a 6-year-old with fever, pallor, petechiae, and peripheral lymphoblasts: what initial labs/imaging are needed, what bone marrow panels are mandatory, and what CNS procedure is performed?
options: A) 1. Stool culture, abdominal X-ray; 2. Hemoglobin electrophoresis; 3. Brain CT

B) 1. Complete Blood Count with differential, peripheral blood film, blood chemistry (uric acid, K, Phos, Ca, LDH), and Chest X-ray; 2. Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy for Morphology, Flow Cytometry (immunophenotyping), Karyotype, and FISH/molecular genetics; 3. Diagnostic Lumbar Puncture with CSF cytospin cytology
C) 1. Urinalysis, renal ultrasound; 2. Skin biopsy; 3. Electroencephalogram
D) 1. Sputum smear, Mantoux test; 2. Lymph node aspiration; 3. Otoscopy
questions.hint: CBC/film/TLS chemistry/CXR; bone marrow morphology, flow cytometry, karyotype, FISH/molecular; lumbar puncture.
questions.explanation: Diagnostic evaluation of acute leukemia requires CBC, chemistry panel for TLS, and Chest X-ray, bone marrow aspirate/biopsy (morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, FISH), and lumbar puncture with CSF cytology for CNS staging.
